title: Metaphors: Helpful Until They Aren’t
editorial_note: Automated dialogue draft from the revised lesson. Review spoken wording and meaning before publishing.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Today we're talking about Metaphors: Helpful Until They Aren’t. By the end, you'll know why this matters, how to use it, and what to notice in a real product.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What is the problem we are trying to understand?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Interface metaphors borrow a familiar domain to help people form an initial model: desktop, inbox, card, cart, folder, timeline. They work when relevant relationships transfer. They fail when designers force the new system to imitate superficial details of the old one or when the borrowed rules produce false expectations.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Why does that happen?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use a metaphor as a teaching aid, not a substitute for a coherent conceptual model. Ask which parts of the analogy are intended to transfer, where it breaks, and how the interface reveals the difference before it causes harm. Direct language and visible system state are often better than a decorative metaphor.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at audit what the metaphor transfers?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: List expectations carried from the source domain: objects, actions, limits, ownership, reversibility, and social meaning. Decide which the product supports and where the mapping breaks. A “trash” suggests recoverability; “wallet” suggests possession and transfer; “assistant” suggests competence and relationship.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use metaphor to accelerate orientation, then teach actual behaviour through labels, structure, status, and examples. Do not extend it into awkward rules merely for purity. Test what people predict in edge cases. Retire or constrain a metaphor when its false expectations outweigh its learning value.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What changes when we look at metaphors in language and ai?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Evaluate a metaphor under stress: multiple simultaneous referrals, delegated access, a rejected request, uncertain timing, and irreversible action. Ask participants what they predict, not whether the design feels intuitive. A metaphor is valuable only while its useful predictions exceed its false ones.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Use metaphor to transfer a useful relationship
turns.text: What changes when we look at use metaphor to transfer a useful relationship?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Metaphors age as products gain capability. A desktop trash can does not naturally explain retention policy, shared ownership, or cloud recovery. The team keeps familiar surface language where it reduces learning, but exposes the actual model when consequences differ.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: It tests prediction and recovery, especially with people whose cultural or technical background may not include the assumed source domain.

turns.speaker: host
turns.act: Document the metaphor’s valid and invalid predictions
turns.text: What changes when we look at document the metaphor’s valid and invalid predictions?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Metaphors are tested across culture, expertise, language, and assistive technology. They can support initial learning while the underlying conceptual model remains explicit. When product capability outgrows the metaphor, the team preserves useful language but stops forcing new behaviour into a misleading analogy.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Where does the harder design decision appear?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Legacy metaphors can hide product strategy. A “file” model may make permission, ownership, versioning, and collaboration harder to design clearly. Retire a metaphor when it prevents the better system from being understood.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should we look at more closely?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Metaphors borrow a familiar domain to make an unfamiliar system easier to approach: a desktop, a shopping cart, a notebook, a queue, or a conversation. They can supply useful expectations about objects and actions, especially during early learning. But every metaphor carries limits.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Digital objects can be copied, searched, shared, versioned, and automated in ways physical objects cannot; extending the comparison too far can create false expectations.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Use a metaphor as a bridge, not a constraint. Identify which parts of the familiar model transfer usefully and where the system must explain its difference. Prefer plain language and visible outcomes when the metaphor obscures consequential behaviour. Test whether people predict the result correctly rather than asking whether they recognise the image or phrase.

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Failure modes to watch

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Decorative metaphor: a visual reference adds style without making action or outcome clearer. False transfer: people assume physical-world rules that do not apply digitally. Mixed metaphors: different parts of the product teach incompatible ways of thinking. Metaphor lock-in: the team preserves an outdated comparison even after it blocks a better conceptual model.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Can we see that in a concrete product situation?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: A “wallet” can suggest personal possession, yet a digital wallet may store credentials rather than money and allow an issuer to revoke them. The metaphor helps entry only if the product makes those authority limits visible.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How does this connect to what we have already learned?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: lesson 15 defined the conceptual model. Metaphor can help a person enter that model, but task analysis in lesson 17 will test whether the actual workflow supports the goal.

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What should I notice the next time I use a product?

turns.speaker: guide
turns.text: Identify a product metaphor and the moment it stops helping. What expectation does it create, and what would explain the product more honestly?
